name: Petrelintide
lead: Petrelintide (development name ZP8396) is an investigational once-weekly injectable amylin analogue discovered and developed by Zealand Pharma for weight management and type 2 diabetes.[1][2] It is aimed at people who want to lose body fat, and so at the changes in body shape, waist size and facial fullness that come with fat loss. Because it works through amylin, a satiety hormone, rather than through the GLP-1 pathway used by semaglutide and tirzepatide, it is being developed both on its own and as a possible partner to incretin drugs.[5][9]

In March 2025 Roche entered an exclusive collaboration with Zealand to co-develop and co-commercialise petrelintide, alone and in a fixed-dose combination with its incretin candidate CT-388 (enicepatide).[1] A phase 1b trial reported in June 2024 weight loss of 8.6 percent over 16 weeks.[1] The 42-week phase 2 trial ZUPREME 1 has since been published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, and phase 3 trials began recruiting in autumn 2026.[4][10][12] Petrelintide is not approved anywhere.

chain: Mimics amylin, a fullness signal released after meals

angle.text: Petrelintide is studied as a weight-loss injection: by increasing the feeling of fullness it reduces food intake, and the resulting loss of body fat changes waist, face and overall physique. It is available only inside clinical trials.

infobox: About 10 percent weight loss at 42 weeks (company-reported)[10]

paras: Petrelintide is being developed as a long-term treatment for obesity and overweight with weight-related conditions, and a separate programme studies it in people who also have type 2 diabetes.[4][7] The loss of body fat that follows reduced food intake is what changes a person's visible shape, which is why obesity drugs are of interest in appearance-focused communities.
It is not available by prescription or through any legal retail route; access is limited to trial participants.

Amylin is co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic beta cells after meals. Reviews describe it as slowing gastric emptying, suppressing glucagon release and promoting meal termination through actions in the brain.[15][16] Petrelintide is a long-acting analogue of human amylin; a medicinal chemistry paper from its developers describes optimising it for chemical stability and potency while allowing formulation at about neutral pH, which is intended to make it suitable for co-formulation with other peptide drugs.[2]

Reviews place petrelintide among a second generation of amylin-based agents alongside cagrilintide, eloralintide and others, noting that they differ in receptor selectivity. Petrelintide is described as a more selective amylin receptor agonist, whereas cagrilintide also engages the calcitonin receptor, a distinction authors suggest may matter for tolerability.[16] The first amylin analogue, pramlintide, was limited by modest efficacy and frequent dosing.[15]
Petrelintide is a large peptide with the molecular formula C185H305N49O61 and a molar mass of about 4,191.8 g/mol.[1]

Two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1 trials (single and multiple ascending dose) assessed safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Investigators reported no serious or severe treatment-emergent adverse events; the most common events were mostly mild gastrointestinal ones, and one participant stopped treatment because of them. Nausea occurred in 16.7 to 33.3 percent of petrelintide recipients versus 16.7 percent on placebo in the multiple-dose obesity cohort.[3]

Company-reported phase 1b data in June 2024 showed 8.6 percent weight loss over 16 weeks.[1] Further phase 1 studies have examined kidney impairment, liver impairment and different drug product concentrations.[17]

ZUPREME 1 was a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 32 sites in Poland, Romania and the United States. Adults without type 2 diabetes who had a BMI of at least 30, or at least 27 with hypertension or dyslipidaemia, were randomised 5:1 to self-injected weekly petrelintide (maintenance doses 1.0 to 9.0 mg) or placebo for 42 weeks including dose escalation; the primary endpoint was percentage change in body weight after 28 weeks.[4] The registry lists 493 participants.[6]

Press coverage of the published results reported on-treatment weight loss at 42 weeks of roughly 8.7 percent at the lowest dose and 10.2 to 10.7 percent at the three highest doses, against about 1.7 percent for placebo, with benefit levelling off at the upper doses. Nausea was reported by 20 percent of petrelintide recipients versus 6 percent on placebo; serious adverse events were 3 versus 4 percent, and about 1.5 percent stopped treatment because of gastrointestinal effects.[10][11] Lead investigator Timothy Garvey was quoted calling it "a well-tolerated medication."[10]

Commentary by Sten Madsbad and Jens Holst said amylin-based therapies might have a future alone or in combination, while noting it is unclear whether the people who get stomach side effects are the same ones who cannot tolerate GLP-1 drugs.[11] The trial ran 42 weeks, did not compare petrelintide directly with semaglutide or tirzepatide, and was funded by the manufacturer; long-term cardiovascular and safety outcomes have not been reported.[10]
ZUPREME 2 enrolled 221 people with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes and has completed.[7]

Phase 3 trials registered in 2026 include a study in overweight or obesity (about 3,900 participants), one in obesity with type 2 diabetes (about 600) and one in obesity with established cardiovascular disease (about 2,500).[12][13][18] A phase 2 dose-finding study pairing petrelintide with enicepatide is registered but not yet recruiting.[14]

Zealand Pharma discovered and developed the compound. Preclinical work in rats was presented in 2022 and a single-ascending-dose trial in 2023.[1] Roche's March 2025 agreement covers co-development and co-commercialisation of petrelintide alone and combined with CT-388; a Reuters headline cited a value of up to 5.3 billion US dollars.[1]
Petrelintide is an unapproved investigational drug with no marketing authorisation. No approval date, price or coverage has been announced.[10]

card.summary: A weekly amylin-analogue obesity drug from Zealand and Roche, now in phase 3.

quick.overview:
Petrelintide is a weekly injectable amylin analogue from Zealand Pharma, partnered with Roche. It targets satiety rather than GLP-1 pathways.

A phase 1b trial reported 8.6 percent weight loss over 16 weeks; phase 2 results were published in 2026.
quick.mechanism: It mimics amylin, a hormone that signals fullness after meals.
quick.risks: Investigational; safety data are in phase 1 and 2 publications. Not approved.
